hints: Calculate the downhill component of weight: $mg\sin\theta = 80(10)(0.04) = 32\text{ N}$.
Driving force balances both forces: $F_D = 24 + 32 = 56\text{ N}$. Use $P = F_D \times v$ with $v = 4\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the constant resistance force from the work done over $25\text{ m}$:
$$F_{\text{res}} = \frac{W_{\text{res}}}{d} = \frac{600}{25} = 24\text{ N}$$

Calculate the component of weight opposing motion down the slope:
$$F_{\text{gravity}} = mg\sin\theta = 80(10)(0.04) = 32\text{ N}$$

At constant speed, driving force balances total opposing force:
$$F_D = F_{\text{res}} + mg\sin\theta = 24 + 32 = 56\text{ N}$$

Calculate power output using $P = F_D \times v$:
$$P = 56 \times 4 = 224\text{ W}$$

teacher_walkthrough: The cyclist climbs the incline at a constant speed of $4\text{ m s}^{-1}$, so acceleration is zero ($a = 0$).

Find the resisting force from the given work done over distance $d = 25\text{ m}$:
$$W_{\text{resistance}} = F_{\text{res}} \times d$$
$$600 = F_{\text{res}} \times 25 \implies F_{\text{res}} = \frac{600}{25} = 24\text{ N}$$

Find the component of weight acting down the incline:
$$W_\parallel = mg\sin\theta = 80 \times 10 \times 0.04 = 32\text{ N}$$

By Newton's first law, the forward driving force $F_D$ must balance resistance plus the component of weight:
$$F_D = F_{\text{res}} + W_\parallel = 24 + 32 = 56\text{ N}$$

Calculate the power output:
$$P = F_D \times v = 56 \times 4 = 224\text{ W}$$

hints: Calculate work done by the cyclist on the horizontal road: $W_{\text{cyclist}} = P \times t = 224 \times 10 = 2240\text{ J}$.
Initial kinetic energy at the top of the hill is $\frac{1}{2}(80)(4^2) = 640\text{ J}$.
Apply the work-energy balance: $\frac{1}{2}(80)v^2 = 640 + 2240 - 1200$, and solve for $v$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the work done by the cyclist during the $10\text{ s}$ period:
$$W_{\text{cyclist}} = P \times t = 224 \times 10 = 2240\text{ J}$$

Calculate initial kinetic energy of the cyclist:
$$E_{k1} = \frac{1}{2}(80)(4^2) = 40(16) = 640\text{ J}$$

Apply the work-energy theorem on the horizontal section:
$$\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = E_{k1} + W_{\text{cyclist}} - W_{\text{res}} = 640 + 2240 - 1200 = 1680\text{ J}$$

Solve for final speed $v$:
$$40v^2 = 1680 \implies v^2 = \frac{1680}{40} = 42 \implies v = \sqrt{42} \approx 6.48\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
teacher_walkthrough: After reaching the top of the hill, the road is horizontal, so gravitational potential energy does not change.

Calculate the work input by the cyclist over $10\text{ s}$ at constant power $P = 224\text{ W}$:
$$W_{\text{cyclist}} = P \times t = 224 \times 10 = 2240\text{ J}$$

Calculate the initial kinetic energy at speed $u = 4\text{ m s}^{-1}$ with $m = 80\text{ kg}$:
$$E_{k1} = \frac{1}{2}mu^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 80 \times 4^2 = 40 \times 16 = 640\text{ J}$$
The work done against resistance during this period is given as $W_{\text{resistance}} = 1200\text{ J}$.

By the work-energy principle, the final kinetic energy equals initial kinetic energy plus work done by the cyclist minus work done against resistance:
$$E_{k2} = E_{k1} + W_{\text{cyclist}} - W_{\text{resistance}}$$
$$\frac{1}{2}(80)v^2 = 640 + 2240 - 1200$$
$$40v^2 = 1680$$
$$v^2 = \frac{1680}{40} = 42$$
$$v = \sqrt{42} \approx 6.4807\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 6.48\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
